titleStmt.title: Relaxing Mixed-Criticality Scheduling Strictness for Task Sets Scheduled with FP

analytic.title: Relaxing Mixed-Criticality Scheduling Strictness for Task Sets Scheduled with FP

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Current trends in the embedded systems field tend to collocate multiple functionalities upon a single computing platform, the aim being to reduce both the size and cost of embedded systems. Nevertheless, it is unlikely that all functionalities share the same level of criticality, and certification of the system has to be achieved using varying degrees of rigorousness. Typically, a task τi is guaranteed to meet its temporal constraints up to a criticality level that is equal to its own criticality. When those conditions are no longer met, i.e. when another higher priority task τj has its execution time that exceeds its Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) w.r.t. the criticality level of τi, a common approach is to suspend τi. However, in some cases, it may not be necessary to suspend tasks with a lower criticality immediately as they could still be executed without compromising the deadlines of high criticality tasks. As a step towards this aim, we propose a method, denoted Latest Completion Time (LCT), that allows lower criticality tasks to proceed with their execution as long as they do not prevent higher criticality tasks from meeting their deadlines. Furthermore, we show that tasks suspension can only be temporary, and prove that a particular definition of idle times can be used to reset the system's criticality level. Finally, we study the performances of our LCT mechanism w.r.t. the classical mechanism that suspends a task as soon as the system criticality level becomes higher than its own criticality.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Our work is driven by the increasing trend in embedded systems towards integrating multiple functionalities on shared resources. In such systems though, all functionalities do not necessarily share a common criticality level. This means that the system may be subject to various certification processes, which are only concerned with the validation of a subset of the functionalities. Furthermore, the certification processes are carried out using analysis methods whose rigor depends on the criticality of the tasks that need to be certified. Mixedcriticality systems are an attempt to model systems that need to be certified at various levels of assurance. In practice, a task that is subject to multiple certification processes will be characterized by multiple estimations of its Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET), some of which are more pessimistic than others. This reflects the differences in rigor adopted by the certification authorities. The more a certification authority wants to ensure a task will never exceed its WCET, the more conservative its estimation will be. Nevertheless, when certifying that a task will meet its constraints, the assurance level that is used for other tasks is equal to the criticality of that particular task. This means that when running the system, if another task is run at a level of assurance that is higher (w.r.t. to its execution duration) than the criticality of the initial task, then this task will be suspended, since the conditions that guarantee its feasibility are no longer met. Nevertheless, this approach can be overly pessimistic, as lower criticality tasks may still have time to complete their execution, or at least to go on with their execution for some time, without compromising the temporal constraints of higher criticality tasks. Therefore, we applied a strategy previously presented for traditional task sets [1], commonly known as sensitivity analysis, and referred to as the allowance in this article, to mixed-criticality task sets. The allowance is meant to avoid, or at worst to delay until the latest time as possible, the rise in criticality level in order to minimize the number of tasks that will miss their deadline. We then present a simple implementation of the allowance that only relies on timers, called the Latest Completion Time (LCT), which is inspired of the Latest Execution Time [1]. Furthermore, we tackle the problem of reducing the criticality of the system. Indeed, if the criticality of the system can be reduced, this means that the number of tasks being ignored will drop. We show that there exists a time when all tasks can be scheduled again.

div.head: A. Related work
div.p: Mixed-Criticality scheduling is an emerging research domain which is gaining increasing interest. Vestal [2] initially introduced the mixed-criticality task model. In his work, he highlighted the difficulty in computing exact WCETs, and observed that in practice, the higher the degree of assurance required that a task will never exceed its WCET, the more conservative the approximation of the latter becomes. This degree of assurance is characterized by a level of criticality. He also suggested a fixed-task-priority strategy based on the Audsley priority assignment scheme [3]. Dorin et al. [4] proved that under the restricted case of independent task systems with constrained-deadlines, Vestal's modified Audsley's approach was optimal in the class of fixed-task priority algorithms. Nowadays, the Mixed-Criticality (MC)-Schedulability problem is commonly known to arise in two different contexts.

The first one is concerned with applications that are subject to multiple certification requirements. In this context, different Certification Authorities (CA) need to validate the application functionalities. Nevertheless, the more critical a functionality is, the more pessimistic the CA will be in the estimation of the WCET. Baruah et al. [5] studied mixed-criticality systems in this context, but restricted their work to a set of mixedcriticality jobs. In particular, Baruah [6] pointed out the intractability of the MC-Schedulability problem, and quantified the fundamental limitations of MC-Scheduling for certification considerations. To tackle the intractability of MC-Scheduling, they suggest two sufficient schedulability conditions, referred to as the WCR-schedulability and OCBP-schedulability conditions. Later, Baruah and Li [7] extended their previous work and suggested a fixed-job-priority scheduling strategy based on their OCBP-schedulability condition. Baruah et al. also adapted the Earliest Deadline First algorithm to mixedcriticality systems, by modifying the deadlines of tasks. This approach is known as EDF-VD. More recently, Guan et al. [8] presented a new approach for scheduling mixed-criticality systems, which relies on an offline fixed-job-priority ordering computation, which is then used on-line by the scheduler. At the same time, Baruah et al. [9] formalized the response time analysis for mixed-criticality tasks. The second context in which mixed-criticality is defined considers that among all functionalities deployed on a single computing platform, some might be more critical, in the sense that they are more important, than others. In this context, Lakshmanan et al. [10], [11] observe that a reservation based approach, meant to isolate functionalities and prevent interferences, might lead to a criticality inversion problem, where a less critical task is favored over a high critical task because the latter exceeded its reserved time partition. They suggested a new approach, termed zero-slack scheduling, to avoid this problem. Sensitivity analysis was previously studied by Bini et al. [12], [13]. They discussed the concept of a feasibility region which allows one to determine the space of possible values for a particular task parameter. The allowance mechanism was initially introduced by Bougueroua et al. [1] in the context of traditional task sets subject to WCET overruns faults. Their work focused on determining the largest value that could be added to a task's WCET such that the whole task set remains schedulable, assuming a sliding window fault model.

div.head: B. This research
div.p: This research focuses on relaxing the strictness that occurs when scheduling mixed-criticality task sets. We suggest improvements that can be implemented in existing on-line scheduling strategies, such that task suspension only occurs when absolutely necessary, thereby allowing more jobs to meet their deadline. We also notice that task suspension can be reversed when the system workload decreases.

div.head: C. Organization of the paper
div.p: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents our model of mixed-criticality task sets. Section III states the intractability of the MC-Schedulability problem and presents a sufficient condition for testing it. This condition serves as a foundation in Section IV to express the underlying idea behind the allowance concept. Section V formally presents the allowance concept, in the context of MC-scheduling, which is further implemented in Section VI. In Section VII, we characterize the set of times when it becomes possible to reset the criticality of the system. Finally, Section VIII analyses the efficiency brought along with our on-line mechanisms.

div.head: II. MODEL AND DEFINITIONS
div.p: Our study focuses on uniprocessor, preemptive systems. We consider mixed-criticality sporadic task sets τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } where the maximum criticality of a task is bound by L. A task in a mixed-criticality system is characterized by a 5-tuple τ i = {R i , T i , D i , χ i , C i } where:
• R i ∈ N is the release time of the first job of task τ i ;
div.formula: • T i ∈ N \ {0} is the period of task τ i ; • D i ∈ N \ {0} is the deadline of task τ i , D i ≤ T i ; • χ i ∈ N is the maximum criticality of the task τ i , χ i ≤ L; • C i ∈ N L is a size L vector of WCETs, where C i ( ) is an estimation of the WCET of task τ i at criticality level ∈ [1, L].

From the specifications of τ i , we can say that c i k ≤ C i (X i ), but the exact value of c i k will not be known until J i k completes its execution. At any time t, we call the j th job J i j released by task τ i available if t ≥ r i j and J i j has not yet completed its execution. The actual execution time of job J i j is not known from the specification of τ i , but will only be discovered when J i j completes its execution. At any time t, we define the scenario s t i of task τ i as the set of exact execution times {c i 1 , c i 2 , ..., c i k } for each of the k jobs J i j released by τ i that already completed their execution at time t. The scenario of the mixed-criticality task set τ at time t is defined as s t = {s t 1 , s t 2 , ..., s t n }. The criticality level of scenario s t is the smallest integer such that, for each s t i ∈ s t , c i k ≤ C i ( ) ∀k. Intuitively, it represents the smallest criticality level such that no task exceeded its WCET for that particular criticality level. If no such exists, then the scenario is said to be erroneous, since at least one task exceeded its WCET at its own criticality level (c i j > C i (χ i )). Definition 1. A schedule for a scenario s t of criticality level is feasible if every job J i j | c i j ∈ s t i , ∀i, with χ i ≥ , receives execution time c i j between its release time and its deadline. This definition implies that mixed-criticality scheduling is only concerned with respecting temporal constraints of tasks of which criticality level is higher than or equal to the criticality level of the scenario. Definition 2. An on-line scheduling policy is correct for a task set τ if, for any non-erroneous scenario of τ , the policy generates a feasible schedule.

Since an on-line scheduling policy discovers the exact execution times of the jobs when they complete their execution, the criticality level of the scenario is not known beforehand. All available jobs are therefore initially scheduled. As soon as a job exceeds its WCET of level -1, the criticality of the scenario is raised to level , all available jobs of criticality lower than are dropped, and future releases from tasks of which criticality is lower than are no longer taken into consideration. Definition 3. A mixed-criticality task set τ is MC-schedulable if it admits a correct on-line scheduling policy.

Figure 1 extends the traditional task state model [14] with additional transitions, or transition labels, to take into consideration the task suspension mechanism. A task can be • Running: a task τ i is running when the scheduler chooses τ i for execution. While being in this state, the instructions of τ i are processed by the CPU. At any time, at most one task will be in the running state. • Ready: a task τ i reaches the ready state if all functional prerequisites for a transition into the running state exist, and τ i is only waiting for election from the scheduler. • Suspended: a task τ i reaches the suspended state if it is currently not a candidate for election from the scheduler. Definition 4. The response time of a job of a task τ i is the amount of time between the time t 1 at which τ i releases the job, and the time t 2 at which this jobs completes its execution in an arbitrary release time scenario, taking into account the workload of higher priority jobs in [t 1 , t 2 ).
Definition 5. The worst-case response time resp i of task τ i is the maximum duration to execute any job of τ i .

From Definition 5, one can easily deduce that resp i ≥ C i (χ i ). Definition 6. A critical instant for a task τ i is defined to be an instant at which τ i releases a job and the response time of that job will be the highest among all jobs released by τ i .

Liu [15] showed that, when considering a traditional task set scheduled with fixed priority (FP), a critical instant for a task τ i occurs whenever τ i releases a job simultaneously with all higher priority tasks τ j and all the jobs of the tasks are released periodically. As shown in theorem 1, this can be extended to mixed-criticality task sets.

Theorem 1. Let τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } be a sporadic mixedcriticality task set scheduled with FP. A critical instant for a task τ i occurs whenever τ i releases a job simultaneously with all higher priority tasks τ j and all the jobs of the tasks are then released periodically Proof: Since each task τ i is certified at criticality levels up to its own criticality X i , we can map each task τ j ∈ τ onto a traditional task τ j , where the WCET of τ j is equal to C j (min(X j , X i )). Since we obtain a traditional task set, the results proved by Liu [15] can be reused, and this proves our theorem.

div.head: III. DETERMINING MC-SCHEDULABILITY
div.p: Baruah et al. [6] proved that the MC-schedulability problem, applied to a finite set of jobs, is NP-hard. Instead of relying on exact MC-schedulability conditions, we will focus on a sufficient condition that can be verified in polynomial time. The algorithm used to verify this condition, introduced by Vestal [2], determines off-line a total ordering of the tasks in τ . Each task is assigned a distinct priority and jobs inherit the priority of the task that released them. At each instant t, the scheduler executes the available job with the highest priority. The priority assignment is realized using the Audsley approach [3] based on the following definition (priority n is the lowest priority and priority 1 the highest). Definition 7. A task τ i in a mixed-criticality task set τ is said to be viable at the lowest priority level if all of the following conditions are satisfied:

1) the lowest priority is assigned to τ i ; 2) all other tasks in τ can be assigned any priority provided that these priorities are higher than the priority assigned to τ i ; 3) every job released by τ i meets its deadline when it is executed for at most C i (χ i ) time units and all other tasks τ j in τ generate jobs that run for at most C j (χ i ) time units.

Algorithm The priority order is then constructed iteratively using algorithm 1, which is known to run in polynomial time [3]. If such a priority order exists, i.e. if a task viable at the lowest priority level is found at each step (w.r.t. the remaining set of unassigned priority tasks), then each task τ i is guaranteed to meet its deadline if it executes for no more than C i (χ i ) time units and no task τ j with a higher priority than τ i executes longer than C j (χ i ) time units.

Because the priority of a task is based on its own criticality level, we say that a task set is Own Criticality Based Priority (or OCPB)-schedulable if we can find a complete ordering of the tasks using algorithm 1.
Theorem 2. If a mixed-criticality task set τ is OCBPschedulable on a given processor, then τ is MC-schedulable on the same processor.
Proof: This proof is the same as the one presented by Baruah et al. [16], but applied to a set of mixed-criticality tasks instead of a set of mixed-criticality jobs.

Example 2. Let us consider again the task set τ presented in example 1. A priority assignment which makes τ OCBP-Schedulable is τ 3 τ 2 τ 1 . Indeed, since τ is a sporadic task set with simultaneous release times, t = 0 is a critical instant for every task, and it follows that one does only need to consider the response time of the first job of each task to determine schedulability. Task τ 1 can be assigned the lowest priority because its response time does not exceed 3 < D 1 time units when neither of the other tasks exceed their WCET at criticality level 1. Task τ 2 can be assigned the middle priority because its response time does not exceed 6 < D 2 time units when task τ 3 does not exceed its WCET at criticality level 2. Finally, task τ 3 can be assigned the highest priority because its response time does not exceed 7 < D 3 time units. Since τ is OCBP-Schedulable, it follows from theorem 2 that τ is also MC-Schedulable.
In the following section, we will focus on task sets which are OCBP-schedulable. Furthermore, SectionV-B assumes fixed priorities to be assigned according to algorithm 1.

div.head: IV. DELAYING CRITICALITY RISING
div.p: Traditional mixed-criticality scheduling policies stop a job as soon as the criticality of the scenario becomes higher than the criticality level of that job. In particular, as soon as the criticality level of the scenario reaches , all tasks τ i with χ i < are suspended, even though they could still run for some time without compromising the temporal constraints of the active jobs of criticality at least . This is because the OCBP-schedulability condition presented in Section III can no longer guarantee their temporal constraints. We argue that this principle is too restrictive and can be relaxed under certain conditions. In the case of task sets that are OCBP-schedulable, the following lemma already allows us to reduce the set of tasks that need to be suspended. Lemma 1. Let τ be a mixed-criticality task set which is OCBP-schedulable, and τ i be any task in the priority order constructed by algorithm 1. When a job released by τ i reaches its WCET at criticality level ≤ X i , it is never necessary to suspend the tasks τ j with χ j < that have a higher priority than τ i .

Proof: Let τ i ∈ τ be a task that reaches its WCET at criticality level . Since τ is OCBP-schedulable, each job released by τ i can execute up to C i (χ i ) time units and still meet its deadline if no higher priority task τ j executes longer than C j (χ i ). Let τ p be a higher priority task, whose criticality χ p is lower than χ i . Since χ i > χ p , C p (χ i ) = C p (χ p ), and the OCBP-schedulability condition guarantees that each job released by τ i will meet its deadline, even though lower criticality tasks that have a higher priority than τ i execute for their WCET at their own criticality level. Therefore, only the lower criticality tasks that have a lower priority than τ i need to be suspended. Definition 8. A task τ i of criticality at least + 1 is subject to a level-execution overrun, if a job released by τ i exceeds its WCET at level . Lemma 1 prevents us from aborting lower criticality tasks that would still have enough time to fully complete their execution, but we could still go further and allow lower criticality tasks that would normally have to be suspended immediately, to proceed with their execution as long as all the jobs are able to meet their deadlines. This would require to determine for how long tasks τ i of criticality at least + 1 could delay the suspension of lower criticality tasks in case of a level-execution overrun. We call this duration the -allowance of task τ i , which is denoted by A i ( ). Based on this allowance, we can determine the latest instant at which criticality has to be raised, since there is no more hope that all lower criticality tasks meet their deadline after.

div.head: V. ALLOWANCE
div.p: The -allowance of a task τ i , the criticality of which is at least + 1, consists in computing the margin in its WCET of level . It represents the maximum execution time that can be added to C i ( ) such that lower criticality tasks τ j can still meet their deadline if they execute up to C j (χ j ) time units and τ i executes for at most C i ( ) + A i ( ) time units. Theallowance of tasks of which the criticality is less than or equal to will be set to zero.

div.head: C. Allowance with EDF
div.p: The allowance principle that was initially introduced by Bougueroua et al. [1] was applied both to Fixed Priority and Earliest Deadline First scheduling strategies, and dealt only with traditional task sets. Nevertheless, as the following proposition states, the Earliest Deadline First scheduling strategy is not optimal for mixed-criticality task sets.

Proposition 2. Every mixed-criticality task set τ that is MC-Schedulable does not necessarily admit Earliest Deadline First as a correct on-line scheduling policy. In other words, EDF is not optimal for mixed-criticality task sets.

Proof: Let τ be the mixed-criticality task set which was proven to me MC-Schedulable in example 2. Figure 2 shows that the criticality of the scenario is not raised soon enough to guarantee the temporal constraint of task τ 3 when all tasks execute for their WCET at their own criticality level.

Since our study will only focus on task sets τ which are OCBP-Schedulable, and because this property does not allow us to determine if Earliest Deadline first is a correct scheduling policy for τ , we will not implement the allowance principle for the Earliest Deadline First algorithm.

div.head: VI. ALLOWANCE IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: We now present an on-line mechanism for the allowance management than can be implemented using traditional timers. We call this mechanism the Latest Completion Time (LCT). Definition 10. Let r i k be the release time of the k th job J i k released by task τ i , with χ i ≥ . LCT i (r i k ) is defined as the Latest Completion Time J i k , if subject to a level-execution overrun, can proceed with its execution without having to drop lower criticality tasks for the system to still respect temporal constraints of tasks of criticality greater than or equal to .

We will now show how to compute the LCT of a task τ i , and this LCT will be used to determine the instant at which lower criticality tasks should be dropped. Let J i k be the k th job released at time r i k by task τ i with criticality χ i ≥ . The Latest Completion Time for J i k at criticality level is computed at time r i k as follows:

We do not initialize such a timer for jobs of which the criticality is equal to , since they will not be subject to a level-execution overrun. If the allowance mechanism had not been used, the criticality of the scenario would have been raised at time instant 1, thus preventing task τ 1 to complete its execution. Similarly, Figure9 illustrates a scenario where τ 3 exceeds its WCET at criticality level 2, but completes its execution soon enough to prevent the interruption of task τ 2 , which still has enough time to complete its execution for a duration equal to its WCET at its own criticality level. If the allowance mechanism had not been used, the criticality of the scenario would have been raised at time instant 3, thus preventing task τ 2 to complete its execution. Finally, Figure10 illustrates the allowance recovery. Indeed, task τ 3 was granted an allowance of one time unit, but completes its execution before making use of it. This allows task τ 2 to make use of two extra time units to complete its execution without having to interrupt task τ 1 .

div.head: VII. RESETTING CRITICALITY
div.p: The mechanism presented in SectionVI allows us to delay the suspension of lower critically tasks until the latest possible time, thus avoiding to drop jobs that would still have enough time to complete their execution. Nevertheless, in some cases, at a given criticality level, a task might need more time to complete its execution than what the allowance offers, and the criticality of the scenario needs to be raised. In this section, we investigate the relevance of keeping lower criticality tasks suspended. We argue that, if it is indeed necessary to suspend lower criticality tasks to guarantee temporal constraints of higher criticality tasks, this decision is not irreversible, and there exists a time at which all tasks can again execute concurrently, whatever their criticality level.

Throughout this section, we will assume that contrary to what Lemma1 suggests, as soon as the scenario's criticality reaches level , every task of criticality less than will be dropped. The definitions and results we present can nevertheless be a adapted to take into account Lemma1. Definition 11. If the current scenario is of criticality level , a level-idle time t on a processor is defined as an instant in time, such that there are no available jobs of criticality at least waiting to be scheduled at time t.
Theorem 6. Let τ be a sporadic mixed-criticality task set which is MC-Schedulable. Whenever a level-idle time occurs in the scheduling of τ , the criticality of the scenario can be reset to level 1.

Proof: Let t idle be the first level-idle time in the scheduling of τ (with t idle > 0). This means that every job released by a task of which the criticality is at least as high as the scenario criticality at time t idle completed its execution, and no job is currently available. Let τ i be any task in τ that had to be dropped before t idle . We need to show that time t idle , every job released by τ i can again receive C i (χ i ) units of execution in any scenario of criticality at most χ i . Let J i be the first job released by τ i at time t i (t i ≥ t idle ). We distinguish two cases: 1) t i is a critical instant for τ i : it follows that the response time of J i will be the highest among all jobs generated by τ i . But since τ is MC-Schedulable, we know that J i will meet its deadline if it executes up to C i (χ i ), and none of the other tasks τ j releases a job that executes for more than C j (χ i ) time units.

2) t i is not a critical instant for τ i : in this case, we know that the response time of J i will be less than or equal to the worst response time of task τ i . But we proved that J i could meet its deadline if it was released at a critical instant. It follows that J i will also meet its deadline if it is released at a non-critical instant.
Once a level-idle time t idle occurs in the scheduling of the task set, the criticality of the scenario is computed from t idle , and not from time 0 as it was the case before.

Example 5. Let us consider again the task set τ presented in example 1, and a possible scenario for this task set illustrated in Figure11. The first job released by task τ 3 completes its execution after 7 time units. The criticality of the scenario reached level 2 at time t = 1, and level 3 at time t = 3, so both τ 1 and τ 2 were dropped. At time t = 7, a level-3 idle time occurs, so the criticality level can be reset to level 1, and the jobs released by τ 1 and τ 2 can be considered again. Task τ 2 releases its next job at time t = 7, but is preempted by task τ 3 at time t = 8. Since τ 3 completed its execution after 3 time units, the criticality of the scenario reached level 2, and task τ 1 had to be dropped. But τ 2 is still able to meet its deadline. At time t = 13, a level-2 idle time occurs, and the criticality level can be reset again. This allows every task to generate a job which is able to meet its deadline.

div.head: VIII. SIMULATIONS
div.p: In this section we compare the performances of three possible solutions to deal with the criticality rising that happens when scheduling mixed-criticality task sets:

1) The traditional approach (TA): as soon as a task τ i exceeds its WCET at criticality level , the criticality of the scenario is raised, and all task τ j with χ j = , having a priority lower than τ i , are dropped.

2) The traditional approach, extended with a criticality decreasing mechanism (CD): as soon as a task τ i exceeds its WCET at criticality level , the criticality of the scenario is raised, and all task τ j with χ j = , having a priority lower than τ i , are dropped. Nevertheless, as soon as a level-idle time occurs, the criticality of the system is reset to its lowest level.

3) The traditional approach, extended with a criticality decreasing mechanism and the allowance concept (CD-A): as soon as a task τ i exceeds its WCET at criticality level plus its allowance, the criticality of the scenario is raised, and all task τ j with χ j = , having a priority lower than τ i , are dropped. Nevertheless, as soon as a level-idle time occurs, the criticality of the scenario is reset to its lowest level.

We did not include the case where the allowance was used alone, since once the system reaches the highest criticality level L, every task of criticality less than L is dropped, and tasks of criticality equal to will never be dropped.

Each job J i k released by a task τ i is assigned an exact duration c e i,k in the interval [1, C i (χ i )], using a triangular distribution. As a job usually does not complete its execution after a very short nor a very long amount of time, but rather after an intermediate one, the use of a triangular distribution is a way to represent this. Indeed, the latter makes it possible to concentrate most of the probabilities around a value called the mode. As Figure12 depicts, for a task τ i , the distribution lower limit is set to 0, the distribution upper limit is set to C i (χ i ), and the distribution mode is equal to Ci(χi)

. This means that a job will most of the time complete its execution after an amount of time close to 33% of its WCET at its own criticality level. We then generate a random number r following that particular distribution, and c e i,k = r . Each job's exact duration is completely independent of the exact duration of the previous jobs released by the same task. A job J i k will complete its execution as soon as the scheduler grants him a total of c e i,k time units, but this duration is not known beforehand by the scheduler.

We analyze task sets τ composed of a number of mixedcriticality tasks |τ | varying between 4 and 8, and with a criticality level bounded by 4. For the CD-A approach, the number of faulty tasks is set to f = |τ |, to make sure the criticality is raised due to a task exceeding its WCET at a particular criticality level plus its allowance, and not because the number of faulty tasks exceeds f . We compared the average number of jobs that had to be dropped for the three methods. We therefore generated 100 mixed-criticality task sets, and we reiterated the simulations for various upper bounds on each task utilization (this upper bound is referred to as U max (τ i )). Figures 13 and 14 depicts the results of those simulations. The x-axis represents the maximum utilization per task U max (τ i ), while the y-axis represents the average percentage of jobs that were dropped. We observe that the criticality decreasing mechanism could reduce the number of dropped jobs by 25% in the worst case, while this reduction could reach more than 30% when each task utilization is low. We furthermore notice that when this mechanism is supplemented with the allowance, the number of dropped jobs could be reduced even more by 5% to 9%.
div.formula: U
div.p: We observe that the lower each task utilization is, the more efficient the allowance mechanism is. This is due to the fact that a higher allowance can be granted to each task.

div.head: IX. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we have studied two principles that allow us to relax the strictness of mixed-criticality tasks scheduling using a fixed priority strategy. Those principles are the allowance on WCETs and the criticality decreasing mechanism. We showed how the allowance could be computed using feasibility conditions relying on the worst-case response time of a task according to a criticality level, and suggested a simple mechanism that implements it denoted LCT. We then proved that idle times could be used to decrease the overall criticality of the system. Experiments furthermore attested that the criticality decreasing mechanism could reduce up to 24% the number of jobs that had to be suspended, while the allowance could decrease this number by an additional 8%.
